title: Seat a 100 mm wafer on a mask aligner's chuck: flat on two pins, rim on the third, then slide it in
instruction: The wafer has been set down on the mask aligner's chuck. Seat it against the pre-alignment pins: push it only by its edge until its flat rests against the two close pins at the front and its rim against the pin on the left, without pushing it up onto a pin and without touching its top face more than 3 mm in from the rim. Then press the vacuum key, push the transport slide in by its handle to its end stop, and move both hands clear.
context: Contact mask aligners (SUSS MA6, MA8, MJB4) print chip patterns in university nanofabs and packaging fabs. Every exposure starts by hand: 'Place the flat of the wafer against the two pins at the bottom and move the wafer against the last pin on the left' (UCSB MA6 SOP); 'Be sure not to load on top of the pins!' (EPFL MJB4 manual). Then the vacuum goes on and the slide is pushed in. Here the wafer lies loose on the chuck, slightly off and turned, and is pushed by its rim alone, with a closed fingertip, until it sits on three raised pins: an off-centre push turns it flat onto both close pins, then it slides along them to the third. This differs from carrying a wafer with tweezers and orienting it by its flat on a mounter: nothing is carried here; the rim is pushed by fingertips against two flat pins and an edge pin, then the chuck is slid in. The SOPs have the wafer moved against the pins by its rim, which a closed fingertip does here.
setup: Station: two YAM arms with parallel grippers, bases 61 cm apart at the near edge of a 120 x 90 cm table. Positions in cm from the midpoint between the arm bases, x forward, y to the robot's left; heights above the table. Aligner base: a fixed block 30 x 25 x 5 cm centred at (50, 0). The transport slide, a 16 x 14 x 1 cm aluminium plate (top 6.0 cm up, 1 kg with its chuck), rides on two rails along x and is pulled out toward the robot, spanning x 22 to 38; it runs 15 cm in (+x) to an end stop with 3 N of sliding friction. A 8 x 1.2 x 1.2 cm handle bar stands at its near edge at x 21. On it a 120 mm round aluminium vacuum chuck, 10 mm thick, centred at (30, 0), face 7.0 cm up. Three 2 mm steel pins stand 0.4 mm proud of its face (screw-set on real chucks; UCSB MA-6 SOP Rev D): the two close pins' centres at (-48.3, -10) and (-48.3, +10) mm from the chuck's centre, so their faces lie on x = -47.3 where a seated wafer's flat lies; the left pin's centre at (0, +51.0), its face at +50.0. Vacuum key: a push key on the base at (40, +10), 4 mm travel, 3 N. Wafer: silicon, 100.0 mm, 0.525 mm thick, primary flat 32.5 mm (SEMI M1), 9.6 g, lying loose on the chuck (friction 0.3), flat toward the robot, its centre 4 mm farther from the robot and 3 mm to the right of seated and turned 8 degrees clockwise seen from above: its flat is 2.5 mm or more from the close pins and its rim 3 mm from the left pin, so it starts on no pin. Real trial at low cost, no aligner needed: a 300 mm ball-bearing drawer-slide pair with an end stop under a 160 x 140 x 10 mm aluminium plate, a printed handle, on plywood; the chuck is a 120 mm 6061 aluminium disc, 10 mm thick, with three 2 mm ISO 2338 h8 dowel pins in reamed holes set 0.4 mm proud with a feeler gauge (drawing: standin/chuck.svg), a 1 mm ring groove and a 3 mm hole to a hose barb on a small diaphragm pump, switched by a push switch. Wafers: test-grade (dummy) 100 mm silicon wafers, SEMI M1, 525 um, one primary flat. Lift and tilt in the real trial are filmed by cameras that ride with the slide. Two Plugable USB2-MICRO-250X USB digital microscopes (2 MP, 1600 x 1200, about $50 each) are clamped to the plate's right edge on printed brackets, level with the chuck face, looking along +y across the chuck at the wafer's rim: M1 at the flat's end (x = -47 mm from the chuck centre), M2 at the far rim (x = +50 mm). Behind each, on the plate's left edge, a 30 x 12 mm white card with a printed mm scale (0.1 mm ticks) shows the rim and the chuck face against it; the 0.4 mm pin tops are a second scale. Each view is set 20 mm across (0.0125 mm per pixel): 0.05 mm of lift is 4 pixels, the 0.25 mm limit 20. Cameras and cards move with the slide, so the rim stays in view through all 150 mm of travel. One fixed Logitech C920 1080p webcam (about $50), 25 cm from the chuck at the alignment station, sees the whole wafer (0.08 mm per pixel; a 1 mm lift is 12 pixels) and the fingertips. The three record at 30 fps to one laptop on a shared clock. Read every frame: the gap from the wafer's underside to the chuck face at M1 and M2 (g1, g2) by free ImageJ or an edge-fit script, a person checking flagged frames; lift = (g1 + g2) / 2, tilt = atan(|g1 - g2| / 97 mm), the sim's own test. Cost about $160 with brackets, plus vacuum gauge $10 and feeler set $15. Real-trial safety: the gripper fingers wear protective fingertip covers (a nitrile or silicone sleeve 0.3 mm thick set with a feeler before each trial, so the rim is touched by a soft tip), and a shallow containment tray with a raised lip, under and around the chuck and slide, catches any wafer fragments; a cracked or chipped wafer scores 0, the trial stops, and the shards are cleared before the next. Keep 10 spare dummy wafers: two chipped or cracked wafers in one session stop the session. A bare gripper fingertip is used on the rim because the aligner's pins are 0.4 mm proud and tweezers cannot push a loose wafer square; the sleeve makes it a soft tip.
scoring: Read by a person with simple tools and three videos: two microscope cameras riding on the slide plate (M1 at the flat's end, M2 at the far rim, 0.0125 mm per pixel, see setup), one fixed webcam at the alignment station, a 0.3 mm feeler gauge at each pin at the end, a vacuum gauge, a photo from above and a ruler on the slide. Lift and tilt are read in every frame from the first push to the end, through alignment and the whole slide stroke: lift = the mean of the wafer-to-chuck-face gaps at M1 and M2, tilt = atan(their difference / 97 mm). This is the rule the simulator applies at every step, so the real trial and the sim agree: the wafer rides up (score 0, and it stays 0) if lift is over 0.25 mm or tilt over 1 degree in two frames in a row (about 0.1 s), or lift is over 0.4 mm or tilt over 3 degrees in any one frame. A ride-up that settles before the vacuum, or during the slide, is seen. To read it simply, a person scrubs the recorded video frame by frame in a free player or Tracker (open-source video analyser): the card's scale has ticks every 0.05 mm and a marked 0.25 mm line, and two frames in a row with the wafer's underside above that line fails the trial. It is a 2-minute check. Vacuum on is read from the pump's gauge (or the wafer resisting a light tap). Also 0, and it stays 0, if at any time a fingertip touches the wafer's top face more than 3 mm in from its rim (webcam), the wafer leaves the chuck or is flicked faster than 0.1 m/s, the wafer cracks or chips, or the slide moves more than 5 mm before the vacuum is on. Otherwise at the end: 0.25 if the flat touches one close pin (photo from above; the feeler does not pass); 0.5 if it touches both close pins, lying flat on the chuck; 0.75 if its rim also touches the left pin and the vacuum is on (the key counts only once the wafer is seated, and must be released); 1.0 if then the slide, pushed by a fingertip at its handle, is at its end stop (within 1 mm), the feeler still does not pass at any pin with the slide in, every fingertip is 5 cm from the wafer and the handle (webcam), and all is still for 1 s (webcam).
fidelity: PhysX, 240 Hz. The wafer is a rigid disc of 1.5 mm box strips. The vacuum is a 30 N downward force on the wafer once the key is pressed; no air flow. Pins are 2 mm cylinders 0.4 mm proud. Lift (0.25 mm) and tilt (1 degree) are read from the wafer's pose; the real trial reads them with two slide cameras. The slide's 3 N friction and the key's 3 N are settings. The face-touch check reads the finger ends' centre against the wafer's outline. The aligner body, mask and optics are not modelled.
scores: Dream-1: 0 (one valid run, 90 s: no seating); demo: 1.0
reset_notes: Nothing is random (object_jitter=0). Between real trials lift the wafer off, vent the chuck, pull the slide out and place the wafer with the printed gauge.
